question: Under the federal Inland Navigation Rules, over how many degrees of the horizon must a power-driven vessel's masthead light show unbroken light?
choice_a: 360 degrees, visible from every direction around the vessel
choice_b: 225 degrees, from dead ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on each side
choice_c: 135 degrees, centered on the vessel's stern
choice_d: 90 degrees, visible only from dead ahead to abeam on either side
explanation: A masthead light is defined as a white light placed over the vessel's fore-and-aft centerline showing an unbroken light over an arc of 225 degrees, from dead ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.21 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Definitions

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules' definitions, each sidelight (red port, green starboard) must show unbroken light over what arc of the horizon?
choice_a: 225 degrees, the same arc as a masthead light
choice_b: 360 degrees, so it is visible in every direction
choice_c: 112.5 degrees, from dead ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on its respective side
choice_d: 67.5 degrees, visible only from dead ahead to abeam
explanation: Sidelights are defined as a green light on the starboard side and a red light on the port side, each showing an unbroken light over an arc of 112.5 degrees from dead ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on its side.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.21 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Definitions

question: How many degrees of arc must a vessel's sternlight cover, and where is it visible from?
choice_a: 225 degrees, the same arc as a masthead light
choice_b: 360 degrees, visible from any direction
choice_c: 112.5 degrees, matching a sidelight's arc
choice_d: 135 degrees, visible 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side of the vessel
explanation: A sternlight is a white light placed as nearly as practicable at the stern, showing unbroken light over an arc of 135 degrees, visible 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side of the vessel.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.21 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Definitions

question: Under the Inland Rules' definitions, vessels under 20 meters in length may combine which lights into one lantern?
choice_a: The red and green sidelights, into a single bi-color lantern carried on the fore-and-aft centerline
choice_b: The masthead light and sternlight, into one lantern at the bow
choice_c: The anchor light and towing light, into one lantern
choice_d: Combining any navigation lights is prohibited regardless of vessel size
explanation: The definitions rule permits vessels under 20 meters to combine their sidelights into one bi-color lantern carried on the centerline of the vessel, rather than two separate side-mounted lights.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.21 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Definitions

question: Under the Inland Rules' visibility-of-lights table, what is the minimum visibility range required for a masthead light on a power-driven vessel that is 15 meters (about 49 feet) long?
choice_a: 6 miles, the range required of vessels 50 meters or more
choice_b: 3 miles, because a vessel under 20 meters in the 12-to-50-meter category is held to the shorter masthead range
choice_c: 1 mile, the same as a sidelight on a small vessel
choice_d: 5 miles, the standard range for the entire 12-to-50-meter category
explanation: For vessels 12 to 50 meters, the masthead light must be visible 5 miles, except that where the vessel is less than 20 meters, only 3 miles is required; a 15-meter vessel falls into that shorter-range exception.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.22 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Visibility of Lights

question: Under the visibility-of-lights table, what is the minimum required visibility range for a sidelight on a power-driven vessel under 12 meters in length?
choice_a: 2 miles
choice_b: 3 miles
choice_c: 1 mile
choice_d: 6 miles
explanation: For vessels under 12 meters in length, the required visibility range for a sidelight is 1 mile, the shortest range in the table.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.22 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Visibility of Lights

question: What alternative lighting configuration may a power-driven vessel under 12 meters in length use instead of separate masthead and sternlights?
choice_a: A single yellow all-round light only
choice_b: Two red lights in a vertical line
choice_c: A tricolor lantern combining a masthead light, sidelights, and sternlight, an option limited to sailing vessels rather than power-driven vessels
choice_d: An all-round white light and sidelights
explanation: A power-driven vessel under 12 meters in length may exhibit an all-round white light and sidelights instead of the standard masthead-light-plus-sternlight configuration.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.23 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Power-Driven Vessels Underway

question: What additional masthead light requirement applies specifically to power-driven vessels 50 meters or more in length?
choice_a: A second masthead light, positioned aft of and higher than the forward one
choice_b: A second sternlight, positioned higher than the first
choice_c: A yellow flashing light visible for 6 miles
choice_d: No additional light -- the requirements are identical regardless of vessel length
explanation: Power-driven vessels 50 meters or more in length must display a second masthead light aft of and higher than the forward masthead light, in addition to sidelights and a sternlight; vessels under 50 meters may omit this second light.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.23 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Power-Driven Vessels Underway

question: Under Rule 25(b), what lantern option is available to a sailing vessel under 20 meters in length, and where is it carried?
choice_a: Only under 12 meters, and the lantern replaces the masthead light of a power-driven vessel
choice_b: The sidelights and sternlight normally required may be combined into one lantern, carried at or near the top of the mast where it can best be seen
choice_c: The combined lantern must be carried at the bow, not the masthead
choice_d: No combined-lantern option exists for sailing vessels of any size
explanation: A sailing vessel under 20 meters in length may combine its sidelights and sternlight into one lantern carried at or near the top of the mast where it can best be seen.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.25(b) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sailing Vessels Underway

question: Besides sidelights and a sternlight, what additional lights may a sailing vessel underway exhibit near the top of the mast, and with what restriction?
choice_a: Two all-round white lights, shown only while anchored
choice_b: A single flashing yellow light, required on every sailing vessel
choice_c: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over green, but not shown together with the combined bi-color/sternlight lantern option
choice_d: Red-white-red all-round lights, the same combination used by a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver
explanation: A sailing vessel underway may additionally exhibit two all-round lights in a vertical line near the masthead, red over green, but these may not be shown together with the combined lantern permitted for vessels under 20 meters.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.25(c) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sailing Vessels Underway

question: If a sailing vessel under 7 meters in length cannot practicably display the lights normally required for a sailing vessel, what must it do instead?
choice_a: It is exempt from showing any light at all
choice_b: It must display a masthead light identical to a power-driven vessel's
choice_c: It must remain at anchor until visibility improves
choice_d: Exhibit an all-round white light, or have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light
explanation: A sailing vessel under 7 meters that cannot practicably show the normally required lights must exhibit an all-round white light, or have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.25 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sailing Vessels Underway and Vessels Under Oars

question: What lighting rule applies to a vessel under oars at night?
choice_a: It may show the lights prescribed for a sailing vessel, but if it does not, it must exhibit an all-round white light or have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, shown in time to prevent collision
choice_b: Vessels under oars are completely exempt from all navigation light requirements
choice_c: It must show red and green sidelights only, with no white light
choice_d: It must display two all-round red lights in a vertical line
explanation: A vessel under oars may show the lights prescribed for a sailing vessel, but if she does not, she must have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern (or all-round white light) showing a white light, exhibited in time to prevent collision.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.25 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sailing Vessels Underway and Vessels Under Oars

question: When a sailing vessel is also being propelled by machinery, what day shape must it display forward, and which vessels are excused from this?
choice_a: A black ball; required on every sailing vessel regardless of size
choice_b: A black conical shape, apex downward; vessels under 12 meters in length are not required to display it
choice_c: A diamond shape; only required on vessels over 50 meters
choice_d: No day shape is required for a vessel under both sail and power
explanation: A vessel proceeding under sail while also being propelled by machinery must display forward a black conical shape, apex downward, though a vessel under 12 meters in length is not required to do so.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.25 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sailing Vessels Underway

question: A trawling vessel's basic lights are two all-round lights in a vertical line, green over white (or two cones apex to apex). What additional masthead light requirement applies, and to which vessels?
choice_a: A second white sternlight, required on every trawler regardless of size
choice_b: A flashing yellow light, required only on vessels under 20 meters
choice_c: A masthead light abaft of and higher than the green light, required for vessels 50 meters or more in length; vessels under 50 meters are not obliged to show it but may do so
choice_d: No additional masthead light is ever authorized for a trawling vessel
explanation: A trawling vessel of 50 meters or more must show a masthead light abaft of and higher than the all-round green light; a vessel under 50 meters is not obliged to show it, though she may do so.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.26(b) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Fishing Vessels

question: A fishing vessel that is not trawling displays two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over white. When must it show an additional all-round white light, and in what direction?
choice_a: Whenever it is fishing at night, regardless of gear length
choice_b: Only when the vessel exceeds 100 meters in overall length
choice_c: Additional lights are never required for a non-trawling fishing vessel
choice_d: When its outlying fishing gear extends more than 150 meters horizontally from the vessel, an additional all-round white light must be shown in the direction of the gear
explanation: A fishing vessel other than one trawling must show an additional all-round white light in the direction of her outlying gear whenever that gear extends more than 150 meters horizontally from the vessel.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.26 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Fishing Vessels

question: What lights and day shapes identify a vessel not under command?
choice_a: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line at night, and two black balls in a vertical line by day
choice_b: A single all-round white light at night, and one black ball by day
choice_c: Red-white-red all-round lights at night, and a ball-diamond-ball combination by day, the signal for a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver
choice_d: Two all-round green lights at night, and two diamonds by day
explanation: A vessel not under command displays two all-round red lights in a vertical line where they can best be seen, and by day, two black balls in a vertical line; sidelights and a sternlight are added if the vessel is making way.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.27(a) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Vessels Not Under Command

question: What lights and day shapes identify a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver?
choice_a: Two all-round red lights and two balls, the same signal used for a vessel not under command
choice_b: Three all-round lights in a vertical line -- red, white, red from top to bottom -- at night, and a ball, diamond, ball combination by day
choice_c: A single flashing yellow light at night and a cone by day
choice_d: Sidelights and a sternlight only, with no special day shape
explanation: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver shows three all-round lights in a vertical line, red-white-red, and by day a ball, diamond, ball combination, in addition to a masthead light, sidelights, and sternlight when making way.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.27(b) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Vessels Restricted in Their Ability to Maneuver

question: When a power-driven vessel is towing another vessel astern and the length of the tow exceeds 200 meters, what additional signals are required beyond the normal towing lights?
choice_a: A second sternlight and a ball shape
choice_b: An all-round red light and a cone shape
choice_c: A third masthead light in a vertical line, in addition to the normal two, and a diamond shape where it can best be seen
choice_d: No additional signals are required regardless of tow length
explanation: A vessel towing astern normally shows two masthead lights in a vertical line, but must show three such lights when the length of the tow exceeds 200 meters, together with a diamond shape where it can best be seen.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.24(a) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Towing and Pushing

question: What must a vessel or object being towed astern display if the length of the tow exceeds 200 meters?
choice_a: A masthead light identical to the towing vessel's
choice_b: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line
choice_c: Nothing extra -- a towed vessel never displays a shape
choice_d: Sidelights, a sternlight, and a diamond shape where it can best be seen
explanation: A vessel or object being towed must show sidelights and a sternlight, and if the length of the tow exceeds 200 meters, a diamond shape where it can best be seen.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.24(e) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Towing and Pushing

question: Under the anchored-vessel rule, what lights must a vessel display, and how does the requirement differ for a vessel under 50 meters?
choice_a: A forward all-round white light (or ball by day) and, at or near the stern and at a lower level, a second all-round white light; a vessel under 50 meters may instead show a single all-round white light where it can best be seen
choice_b: Only a single red light at the bow, regardless of vessel length
choice_c: Two all-round green lights in a vertical line
choice_d: A vessel at anchor need not show any light if it is moored to a private dock
explanation: A vessel at anchor must show a forward all-round white light and a second, lower one near the stern (or a ball by day forward), but a vessel under 50 meters in length may instead exhibit a single all-round white light where it can best be seen.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.30(a) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground

question: What additional lighting requirement applies to a vessel 100 meters or more in length while at anchor?
choice_a: It must show a flashing yellow light visible for 6 miles
choice_b: It must use available working or equivalent lights to illuminate its decks
choice_c: It must sound its whistle continuously through the night
choice_d: No additional requirement applies beyond the standard anchor lights
explanation: A vessel of 100 meters or more in length must also use available working or equivalent lights to illuminate her decks while at anchor.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.30(a) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground

question: Which anchored vessels are exempt from the anchor-light requirement under the Inland Rules?
choice_a: Any vessel under 20 meters, regardless of where it is anchored
choice_b: No vessel is ever exempt from anchor lights
choice_c: A vessel under 7 meters in length, when anchored outside a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or area where other vessels normally navigate
choice_d: Any sailing vessel, regardless of length
explanation: A vessel under 7 meters in length is exempt from the anchor-light requirement when anchored outside a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or a place where other vessels normally navigate.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.30 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground

question: Besides her anchor lights, what must a vessel aground display if practicable, and which vessels are excused from this extra signal?
choice_a: A single flashing blue light; every vessel, regardless of size, must display it
choice_b: A diamond shape only, required on every vessel aground
choice_c: Nothing beyond her ordinary anchor lights is ever required
choice_d: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line, plus three balls in a vertical line; a vessel under 12 meters in length is not required to display these
explanation: A vessel aground must show her anchor lights plus, if practicable, two all-round red lights in a vertical line and three balls in a vertical line; a vessel under 12 meters in length is excused from this extra signal.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.30 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground

question: Under the Inland Rules' sound-signal equipment requirements, at what vessel lengths must a whistle, a bell, and a gong (in addition to bell and whistle) be carried?
choice_a: A whistle at 12 meters or more, a bell in addition at 20 meters or more, and a gong (with a tone that cannot be confused with the bell) in addition at 100 meters or more
choice_b: A whistle at 20 meters, a bell at 50 meters, and a gong at 100 meters
choice_c: All three devices are required on every vessel regardless of length
choice_d: A gong is required first, then a bell, then a whistle, as vessel length increases
explanation: A vessel of 12 meters or more must carry a whistle; one of 20 meters or more must also carry a bell; one of 100 meters or more must also carry a gong whose tone cannot be confused with the bell.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.33 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Equipment for Sound Signals

question: In restricted visibility, what sound signal must a power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way through the water sound, and how often?
choice_a: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, the same signal used while making way
choice_b: Two prolonged blasts in succession, with an interval of about 2 seconds between them, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_c: Three short blasts, repeated every minute
choice_d: No sound signal is required once a vessel has stopped
explanation: A power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way through the water sounds two prolonged blasts in succession, with about a 2-second interval between them, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.35(b) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility

question: In restricted visibility, what sound signal must a vessel not under command, restricted in her ability to maneuver, constrained by her draft, sailing, engaged in fishing, or engaged in towing or pushing another vessel sound, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes?
choice_a: One prolonged blast alone, the signal reserved for a power-driven vessel making way
choice_b: Rapid ringing of the bell for about 5 seconds
choice_c: One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts, in succession
choice_d: Five or more short, rapid blasts
explanation: A vessel not under command, restricted in her ability to maneuver, constrained by her draft, sailing, fishing, or towing/pushing sounds one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, in restricted visibility.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.35(c) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility

question: If a vessel being towed is manned, what sound signal must it give in restricted visibility, and when?
choice_a: The identical signal as the towing vessel, sounded at the same instant
choice_b: Five short, rapid blasts
choice_c: A manned towed vessel gives no signal of its own
choice_d: One prolonged blast followed by three short blasts, sounded immediately after the towing vessel sounds its own signal
explanation: A manned vessel being towed sounds one prolonged blast followed by three short blasts, given immediately after the towing vessel sounds her own restricted-visibility signal.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.35(d) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility

question: In restricted visibility, how must a vessel at anchor signal her position, and what additional whistle signal may she sound as a warning?
choice_a: By ringing the bell rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute (with a gong sounded after the bell on vessels 100 meters or more), and she may additionally sound one short, one prolonged, and one short blast to warn an approaching vessel of her position
choice_b: By sounding one prolonged blast every 2 minutes, identical to a vessel underway
choice_c: By sounding five short, rapid blasts continuously
choice_d: An anchored vessel is never required to make any sound signal
explanation: A vessel at anchor rings her bell rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute (with a gong added on vessels 100 meters or more), and may also sound one short, one prolonged, and one short blast to warn an approaching vessel of her position.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.35(f)-(g) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility

question: What must a vessel aground sound in restricted visibility, in addition to the anchor bell (and gong, if 100 meters or more)?
choice_a: Five short, rapid blasts on the whistle only
choice_b: Three separate and distinct strokes on the bell, sounded immediately before and immediately after the rapid ringing
choice_c: One prolonged blast every 2 minutes, with no bell signal
choice_d: No additional signal beyond the ordinary anchor signal
explanation: A vessel aground gives the anchor bell (and gong) signal, plus three separate and distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and immediately after the rapid ringing.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.35(h) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility

question: What alternative is available to a vessel between 12 and 20 meters in length regarding the anchor/aground bell signal in restricted visibility?
choice_a: It is completely exempt from all restricted-visibility sound signals
choice_b: It must use a gong instead of a bell
choice_c: It may substitute some other efficient sound signal for the bell signal, sounded at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_d: It must sound five short blasts instead of ringing a bell
explanation: A vessel of 12 to 20 meters in length is not obliged to give the bell signal but may instead give some other efficient sound signal, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, while anchored or aground in restricted visibility.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.35 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility

question: When power-driven vessels in sight of one another are meeting or crossing within half a mile, what do one, two, and three short blasts mean under the Inland Rules' maneuvering signals?
choice_a: One short blast means turning to starboard, two short blasts mean turning to port, and three short blasts mean the vessel is anchoring
choice_b: These signals are used only in restricted visibility, never when vessels are in sight of one another
choice_c: One, two, and three short blasts all carry the identical meaning: 'proceed with caution'
choice_d: One short blast means 'I intend to leave you on my port side'; two short blasts mean 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side'; three short blasts mean 'I am operating astern propulsion'
explanation: When power-driven vessels in sight of one another are meeting or crossing within half a mile, one short blast means 'I intend to leave you on my port side,' two short blasts mean 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side,' and three short blasts mean 'I am operating astern propulsion.'
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.34(a) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Maneuvering and Warning Signals

question: Under the Inland Rules' maneuvering-and-warning-signal rule, when must a vessel sound the danger/doubt signal of at least five short, rapid blasts, and what may supplement it?
choice_a: Immediately, when a vessel fails to understand the intentions or actions of another vessel, or is in doubt whether sufficient action is being taken to avoid collision; the whistle signal may be supplemented by light flashes
choice_b: Only after a collision has already occurred
choice_c: Only while the vessel is anchored overnight
choice_d: It is purely optional and never required by rule
explanation: The danger signal of at least five short, rapid blasts must be sounded immediately whenever a vessel fails to understand another vessel's intentions or actions, or doubts whether enough action is being taken to avoid collision; it may be supplemented with light flashes.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.34(d) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Maneuvering and Warning Signals

question: When one power-driven vessel intends to overtake another and they are in sight of one another, what whistle signals indicate the overtaking vessel's intended side of passage?
choice_a: The overtaking vessel never sounds a signal -- only the vessel being overtaken signals
choice_b: One short blast means 'I intend to overtake you on your starboard side'; two short blasts mean 'I intend to overtake you on your port side'; the vessel being overtaken sounds a similar signal if in agreement
choice_c: Two prolonged blasts always mean overtaking on the starboard side
choice_d: The signals are identical to the restricted-visibility signals for a vessel underway
explanation: A power-driven vessel intending to overtake another, when in sight of one another, sounds one short blast to mean 'I intend to overtake you on your starboard side' or two short blasts for the port side; the vessel being overtaken sounds a similar signal if in agreement.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.34(c) (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Maneuvering and Warning Signals

question: Under the Inland Rules, when may vessels dispense with sounding whistle signals to indicate their maneuvering intentions to one another?
choice_a: Whenever visibility is good, regardless of any radio communication
choice_b: Whistle signals may never be replaced by radio communication under any circumstance
choice_c: When they have agreed on the manner of passing by radiotelephone, in the circumstances specified by the rule, though they remain free to sound whistle signals as well
choice_d: Only when both vessels are anchored
explanation: Vessels that have agreed on the manner of passing by radiotelephone, under the circumstances specified in the rule, are not obliged to sound the whistle signals otherwise required, though they may still choose to do so.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.34 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Maneuvering and Warning Signals

question: Under the Inland Rules' sound-signal definitions, how long is a 'short blast' and how long is a 'prolonged blast'?
choice_a: A short blast lasts 4 to 6 seconds; a prolonged blast lasts about 1 second
choice_b: Both a short blast and a prolonged blast last exactly 2 seconds
choice_c: A short blast lasts 10 seconds and a prolonged blast lasts 30 seconds
choice_d: A short blast lasts about 1 second; a prolonged blast lasts from 4 to 6 seconds
explanation: A short blast is defined as a blast of about 1 second's duration, and a prolonged blast is defined as a blast of from 4 to 6 seconds' duration.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.32 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Definitions

question: What lights identify a vessel engaged on pilotage duty, and what must it add when underway?
choice_a: Two all-round lights in a vertical line near the masthead, white over red; when underway it also shows sidelights and a sternlight
choice_b: A single flashing blue light at the masthead, with no other lights required
choice_c: Red over green all-round lights, the same as a sailing vessel's optional tricolor
choice_d: Two all-round green lights in a vertical line, with no additional lights when underway
explanation: A vessel engaged on pilotage duty shows two all-round lights in a vertical line at or near the masthead, the upper white and the lower red; when underway, she additionally shows sidelights and a sternlight, and when anchored, the anchor light or shape prescribed for anchored vessels.
source_note: 33 CFR Section 83.29 (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules), Pilot Vessels
